content: The medication contains the hormone progesterone, which plays a critical role in supporting pregnancy by promoting mammary gland development, inducing changes in the endometrium, relaxing uterine smooth muscles, and maintaining pregnancy. It is commonly used in women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART) or those with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss. For women with partial or complete ovarian failure, the recommended dose is 90 mg of an 8% vaginal gel administered twice daily. This treatment may continue for 10 to 12 weeks post-conception until placental autonomy is achieved. If no response is observed with a lower dose (45 mg of a 4% vaginal gel every other day for six doses), the higher dose of 90 mg every other day for six doses may be attempted. However, the vaginal insert is not recommended for use with other vaginal products, such as antifungal medications, as this may interfere with progesterone release and absorption. Common side effects include breast enlargement (40%), breast tenderness (27%), somnolence (27%), cramps (15–26%), mood swings (22–23%), nausea (6–22%), depression (11–19%), dizziness (15–24%), sleep disorders (18%), perineal pain (17%), nervousness (16%), urinary difficulties (11%), musculoskeletal pain (12%), headache (13%), breast pain (13%), abdominal pain (5–12%), constipation (2–3%), cough (8%), vaginal discharge (10%), chest pain (7%), fatigue (8%), irritability (8%), worry (8%), and diarrhea (7–8%). Rare side effects include bloating, vaginal candidiasis, general pruritus, ectopic pregnancy, dysarthria, jaundice, and a drunk feeling. There is also an increased risk of invasive cancer in postmenopausal women using conjugated estrogens combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate. Progesterone therapy is not recommended for the prevention of dementia in older women when combined with estrogens, as it may increase the risk of dementia. It is also not indicated for the prevention of vascular disease. Estrogen therapy should be administered for the shortest duration possible. Contraindications include hypersensitivity to the drug or its excipients, known or suspected malignancy of the breast or genital organs, active arterial or venous thromboembolism, severe thrombophlebitis, liver disease or tumors, undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding, missed abortion, or ectopic pregnancy. Caution is advised in patients with a family history of breast cancer, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), or pulmonary embolism (PE), as well as those with a history of depression, endometriosis, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, renal or hepatic impairment, bone metabolic disease, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), or conditions exacerbated by fluid retention (e.g., migraines, asthma, epilepsy). Physicians should monitor for early signs of thrombotic disorders, such as thrombophlebitis, cerebrovascular disorders, pulmonary embolism, or retinal thrombosis. If any of these occur, the drug should be discontinued immediately. A pre-treatment physical examination should include a thorough evaluation of the breast and pelvic organs, as well as a Papanicolaou smear. Discontinue the medication if jaundice, visual problems (e.g., contact lens intolerance), signs of venous thromboembolism (VTE), severe migraines, significant blood pressure increases, or severe depression develop. The medication should also be discontinued four weeks before major surgery or prolonged immobilization. Patients on warfarin or oral anticoagulants may require an increased anticoagulant dose. Some studies suggest an increased risk of breast cancer with oral contraceptive (OCP) use, particularly with long-term use (five or more years), while other studies show no change in risk. Risk factors include early onset of menstruation (before age 12), late menopause (after age 55), first childbirth after age 30, and nulliparity. Long-term OCP use may also increase the risk of liver cancer. Patients should not use other intravaginal medications within six hours before or after progesterone vaginal therapy. In cases of breakthrough bleeding, non-functional causes should be considered, and adequate diagnostic measures should be undertaken. Patients with a history of depression should be closely monitored. Pathologists should be informed of progesterone therapy when relevant specimens are submitted. Progesterone therapy may decrease glucose tolerance in a small percentage of patients, and diabetic patients should be carefully observed. The medication is classified as Pregnancy Category A, indicating no evidence of fetal risk in controlled studies. However, it should only be used during pregnancy as directed by a physician. The drug passes into breast milk, so caution is advised during lactation. Drug interactions may alter the effectiveness of medications or increase the risk of serious side effects. Patients should maintain a list of all medications and share it with their healthcare provider. Overdose may be harmful if swallowed, and emergency medical attention should be sought in such cases. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered, but patients should not exceed the prescribed daily dose. The medication should be stored at room temperature and properly discarded when expired or no longer needed.
